A church on the north side of the Piazza del Popolo in Rome, beside the city gate where the Via Flaminia arrives from the north, so for centuries it was the first church most travellers saw on entering the city. Legend says Pope Paschal II founded a chapel here in 1099 to drive out demons haunting a walnut tree over the tomb of Nero; the story is first recorded centuries later and has little basis. The church has been held by the Augustinian friars since the mid 13th century, and Martin Luther, a young Augustinian, visited it on his journey to Rome around 1510. Pope Sixtus IV had it rebuilt from the ground in 1472 to 1477 as a three-aisled Latin cross with an octagonal dome, an early Renaissance church whose architect is unknown.

His nephew Pope Julius II had Donato Bramante add a long choir in 1505 to 1510, with a vault painted by Pinturicchio and stained glass by Guillaume de Marcillat. For the banker Agostino Chigi, Raphael designed the Chigi Chapel from about 1512, a domed octagon with his mosaics of the Creation of the World. It stood unfinished until Fabio Chigi, later Pope Alexander VII, had Bernini complete it in the 1650s with statues of Habakkuk and the Angel and of Daniel and the Lion. Bernini also remade the whole church in Baroque style from 1658, changing the front, opening larger windows and adding stucco and statues.

The Cerasi Chapel, designed by Carlo Maderno in 1600 to 1601, holds two canvases by Caravaggio, the Conversion of Saint Paul and the Crucifixion of Saint Peter, the most important paintings in the church, on each side of an Assumption of the Virgin by Annibale Carracci. Between 1816 and 1824 Giuseppe Valadier rebuilt the square in front in Neoclassical style and pulled down the old friary, hiding the church's right side behind a smaller new one.
